title: Bow a sand-covered metal plate like a violin and the sand draws the sound

cover.alt: A brass plate on a wooden stand, its surface dusted with fine sand gathered into curving lines, with a violin bow resting against its edge.
cover.credit: Estes Objethos Atelier, photo Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0

body: When a violin bow is drawn along the edge of a metal plate, the plate vibrates in a pattern: some regions shake hard while the lines between them stay perfectly still. Sand sprinkled on top is flung off the moving regions and **piles up along the still lines**, called nodal lines, drawing a figure of the vibration. A different note makes a different pattern. The German physicist Ernst Chladni, sometimes called the father of acoustics, published the method in 1787, and these shapes are still known as Chladni figures.

slides.prompt: Robert Hooke saw patterns like these a century before Chladni. What did he sprinkle on his plate?
slides.detail: In 1680 Hooke drew a violin bow along a glass plate covered with flour. Chladni’s version used sand on metal.

steps.label: A bow sets the plate vibrating
Patches shake while lines between stay still
Sand is flung off the shaking patches
It settles on the still lines as a figure

slides.alt: Four brass plates of different shapes, including a star and two hexagons, on turned wooden posts, each covered in its own pattern of sand lines.
slides.caption: Every plate shape and every note gives its own figure. These are from the Matemateca collection at the University of São Paulo.
slides.credit: Estes Objethos Atelier, photo Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0

events.text: Hooke sees nodal patterns in flour
He demonstrates it in Paris to Napoleon
Sophie Germain wins it on her third try

slides.heading: Napoleon’s prize
slides.text: Napoleon set a prize for the best mathematical explanation of the patterns. [Sophie Germain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Germain)’s entry was the only one with the right approach, and on her third attempt she became the first woman to win a prize from the Paris Academy of Sciences.

slides.heading: Still in the workshop
slides.text: Variations of Chladni’s technique are still commonly used in designing and building acoustic instruments such as violins, guitars and cellos.

slides.question: Where on the vibrating plate does the sand end up?
slides.explanation: The shaking regions throw the sand off, and it comes to rest along the nodal lines, where there is no vibration at all.
